title: AUD U2·W1 — Audit Evidence & Procedures (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the audit runs on evidence

AUD Unit 1 set risk, materiality, and internal control. Now the auditor must gather evidence to support an opinion on MBG's statements. The standard is sufficient appropriate audit evidence, gathered with a defined set of procedures, and documented well enough that an experienced auditor with no prior connection could follow it. This week is the evidence engine of the audit.

Sufficient appropriate evidence

Two dimensions govern evidence. Sufficiency is the quantity — more is needed as the risk of material misstatement rises and as the quality of each item falls. Appropriateness is the quality, made of relevance (does it address the specific assertion?) and reliability (can it be trusted?). The two interact: highly reliable evidence reduces how much is needed, but no amount of low-quality evidence substitutes for relevance. The auditor seeks reasonable, not absolute, assurance, so evidence is usually persuasive rather than conclusive.

The reliability hierarchy

Reliability rises with independence and directness. Evidence is more reliable when it is obtained from independent sources outside the entity, generated under effective internal control, in documentary (especially original) form, and obtained directly by the auditor rather than through the client. So an external bank confirmation outranks a client-prepared schedule, the auditor's own physical count outranks management's representation, and an original invoice outranks a photocopy. Knowing this ranking lets the auditor choose the most convincing procedure for a high-risk assertion.

The audit procedures

The toolbox of procedures, each suited to particular assertions: inspection of records or assets; observation of a process (watching the inventory count); inquiry of personnel (rarely sufficient alone); external confirmation from third parties; recalculation of mathematical accuracy; reperformance of a control or procedure independently; and analytical procedures. The auditor matches the procedure to the assertion — physical inspection tests existence, while tracing source documents into the records tests completeness; vouching from the records back to source documents tests occurrence/existence. Direction of testing is itself an exam point.

External confirmations

Confirmations are powerful because the evidence comes directly from an independent third party. A positive confirmation asks the recipient to respond whether or not they agree, and is used for larger or riskier balances; a negative confirmation asks for a response only if they disagree, and is appropriate only when risk is low, the population is many small homogeneous balances, and a low exception rate is expected. The auditor controls the confirmation process end to end — preparing, sending, and receiving replies directly — and investigates non-responses with alternative procedures (subsequent cash receipts, shipping documents for receivables).

Substantive analytical procedures

Analytical procedures evaluate financial data through plausible relationships and can serve as substantive evidence. The auditor develops an independent expectation (precise enough to detect a material misstatement), defines a tolerable difference, compares the expectation to the recorded amount, and investigates significant differences with corroboration — not by simply accepting management's explanation. They work best for accounts with predictable relationships (a construction company's payroll-tax expense should track wages; interest expense should track average debt and rates). Recall that analytics are required in planning and again in the final review, and optional as a substantive procedure.

Auditing accounting estimates and fair value

Estimates — the allowance for doubtful accounts, warranty reserves, the percentage-of-completion cost-to-complete, and fair values — carry measurement uncertainty and management bias risk, so the auditor responds with specific approaches: test how management made the estimate (its data, assumptions, and method), develop an independent estimate to compare, or review subsequent events that confirm the estimate. The auditor also evaluates whether estimates show a pattern of bias in one direction across the statements — a possible indicator of fraud. For a contractor, the cost-to-complete estimate is the single most judgmental number on the statements and gets the most attention.

Audit documentation

The work is only as good as its documentation. Working papers must let an experienced auditor with no prior connection understand the nature, timing, and extent of procedures, the results and evidence obtained, and the conclusions reached — including who performed and reviewed the work and when. Documentation is the auditor's defense and the basis for the engagement quality review. Standards set a retention period (generally five years for nonissuers, seven for issuers under PCAOB rules) and a documentation completion window after the report date, after which changes must be tracked.

Using the work of others

The auditor may rely on others but remains solely responsible for the opinion. When using a management's specialist (an appraiser the client hired), the auditor evaluates the specialist's competence, objectivity, and the appropriateness of their work as audit evidence. An auditor's specialist assists the audit team directly. The internal audit function may be used to obtain evidence or provide direct assistance if it is competent and objective, but the external auditor cannot delegate judgments about significant risks. These rules let the audit reach specialized areas — like valuing MBG's real estate — without the auditor personally being an expert in everything.

Audit data analytics and the evolving evidence mix

Modern audits increasingly use audit data analytics (ADA) — analyzing entire populations rather than samples to identify outliers, unusual journal entries, and relationships. A 100% test of journal entries for management-override risk, a three-way match across the full purchase population, or a regression linking revenue to operational drivers can be both more effective and more efficient than traditional sampling. ADA does not change the evidence standards — the results still must be relevant and reliable, and exceptions must be investigated — but it shifts the auditor's work from selecting items to evaluating anomalies. The auditor must still assess the reliability of the data used, because analytics on flawed data produce confident but wrong conclusions.

Evaluating evidence and the iterative audit

Evidence gathering is not linear. As procedures surface results, the auditor reassesses risk: an unexpected analytic result or a confirmation exception may reveal a risk not identified in planning, requiring additional procedures. The auditor accumulates identified misstatements, distinguishing factual (clearly wrong), judgmental (a difference in an estimate), and projected (extrapolated from a sample) misstatements, and aggregates them against materiality. Evidence that contradicts earlier conclusions cannot be ignored — professional skepticism requires the auditor to resolve inconsistencies rather than rationalize them away.

CMA bridge

AUD Unit 1 set the risk and control framework; this week is where the auditor responds to that risk with evidence. The estimate-auditing rules apply directly to the percentage-of-completion cost-to-complete that CMA's WIP accounting produces — the auditor tests the very estimate the management accountant prepares.

Practice and recap

  1. Gather sufficient (quantity) appropriate (relevance + reliability) evidence for reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
  2. Rank reliability: external > internal, auditor-obtained > client-provided, original > copy, under good controls > weak.
  3. Match procedures to assertions (inspect existence, trace completeness, vouch occurrence); use positive vs negative confirmations appropriately.
  4. Audit estimates by testing data/assumptions/method or building an independent estimate; document so an experienced auditor could re-perform; use specialists/internal audit without delegating responsibility.

Recap: the opinion rests on sufficient appropriate evidence, weighted by a reliability hierarchy that favors external, auditor-obtained, original documents; procedures are matched to assertions and confirmations come straight from third parties; substantive analytics test predictable relationships; estimates and fair values demand special skepticism; and everything is documented so an experienced auditor with no prior connection could follow it.

flashcards.back: Sufficiency = quantity (rises with risk, falls with quality); appropriateness = quality = relevance + reliability.
More reliable when external > internal, auditor-obtained > client-provided, original > photocopy, and produced under effective controls.
Vouch from records back to source documents = existence/occurrence; trace from source documents into records = completeness.
Positive: respond whether or not you agree (riskier balances). Negative: respond only if you disagree (low risk, many small homogeneous balances, low expected exceptions).
Develop a precise independent expectation, set a tolerable difference, compare to recorded amount, and corroborate significant differences.
Test management's data/assumptions/method, develop an independent estimate, or review subsequent events; watch for one-directional bias.
Sufficient for an experienced auditor with no prior connection to understand procedures, evidence, and conclusions; retained 5 years (nonissuer) / 7 (issuer).

flashcards.back: The auditor may use them but remains solely responsible for the opinion and cannot delegate judgments on significant risks.

questions.q: Appropriateness of audit evidence refers to its:
questions.explain: Appropriateness is the quality of evidence — its relevance to the assertion and its reliability.

questions.q: Which is the MOST reliable audit evidence?
choices: A bank confirmation received directly by the auditor
questions.explain: External, auditor-obtained, original documentary evidence ranks highest in reliability.

questions.q: Tracing source documents forward into the accounting records tests:
questions.explain: Tracing from source documents into the records tests completeness; vouching the other direction tests existence/occurrence.

questions.q: A negative confirmation is appropriate when:
choices: Risk is low, balances are many/small/homogeneous, and few exceptions are expected
questions.explain: Negative confirmations suit low-risk, numerous small homogeneous balances with a low expected exception rate.

questions.q: A substantive analytical procedure requires the auditor to:
choices: Develop an independent expectation precise enough to detect a material misstatement
questions.explain: The auditor forms a precise expectation, sets a tolerable difference, and corroborates significant differences.

questions.q: When auditing an accounting estimate, the auditor may:
choices: Test the data, assumptions, and method, or develop an independent estimate
questions.explain: Estimates are audited by testing how management made them, building an independent estimate, or reviewing subsequent events.

questions.q: When the auditor uses the work of a specialist, the auditor:
choices: Remains solely responsible for the opinion
Shares the opinion with the specialist
Need not evaluate the specialist's work
questions.explain: The auditor may use a specialist but retains sole responsibility for the audit opinion.
